A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching title, authors and central critique. All pages are readable and support comparison. v1 ends with references and has no appendices; v2 includes Appendices A–C.

before.justification: v1 contains conceptual diagrams, theoretical propositions and analytical examples. Its discussion of empirical estimator failures explicitly attributes those results to earlier work.

after.justification: v2 reports original Gaussian-process and conjugate-model computations in Figures 3–4, documented in Appendix C. Figure 5 additionally reports active-learning outcomes.

M1.justification: The proposed uncertainty-estimation framework expands from predictive entropy and BALD-based estimators to loss-derived uncertainty and policy-dependent expected uncertainty reduction. v2 Sections 5.1–5.3 introduce an estimator with separate proxies for future-data generation and model updating, substantially broadening the framework’s inputs and computations.

E1.justification: v1 has no original experimental coverage. v2 adds a Gaussian-process regression example, Bernoulli and Gaussian prediction simulations, and active learning on Curated MNIST and Coarse ImageNet (Figures 3–5 and Appendix C).

E2.justification: Figure 5 introduces evaluated comparisons among BALD, predictive-entropy acquisition and random acquisition on both image tasks. v1 discusses acquisition methods but reports no experimental comparator set.

E3.justification: v2 introduces experimental protocols: a two-point Gaussian-process example evaluated under two losses; exact conjugate inference at n = 1, 10, 100 and 1000 using squared estimation errors; and test negative log likelihood versus acquired labels. These are new settings, not revisions of experiments reported in v1.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantive diagnostic analyses: Figure 3 tests how uncertainty, predictive performance and data dispersion differ under two losses; Figure 4 examines sample-size sensitivity and compares short-run versus long-run information-gain estimation errors. v1 offers analytical discussion and cites external findings instead.

E5.justification: Figure 4 and Appendix C.2 newly specify averaging over 50 repeats with different random-number seeds and display predictions across seeds. v1 contains no corresponding repeated-run or statistical reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds all empirical result curves. They demonstrate distinct uncertainty/performance/dispersion behavior, smaller short-run than long-run information-gain estimation errors in the studied conjugate models, and BALD’s advantage over entropy acquisition in Figure 5. These are newly reported findings, not same-setting performance improvements over v1.

T1.justification: v2 generalizes the entropy decomposition to loss- and policy-dependent expected uncertainty reduction, adds scoring-rule and discrepancy derivations, and establishes additional Bayes-estimator results. v1’s first two propositions correspond to v2’s Propositions 4–5 with explicit posterior-concentration assumptions. Proposition 6 and the derivations in Appendices A–B substantially extend the theory.

C1.justification: The central critique of aleatoric–epistemic terminology is retained. However, v1’s contribution of a minimal entropy-based clarification becomes a broader claimed unification of uncertainty, predictive performance and data dispersion through decision theory. v2 also makes explaining BALD’s practical acquisition utility a principal contribution.

C2.justification: v2 explains errors arising from simulated future data and approximate model updating, deemphasizes infinite-data decompositions for practical acquisition, and proposes a short-run explanation of BALD’s usefulness. It adds substantive qualifications about loss choice, imperfect reference systems and the non-universality of the observed estimation-error ranking.

D1.justification: New Appendix C supplies Gaussian-process training points, kernel and noise scale, reference distributions, conjugate-model specifications and error calculations. It also provides a code link for Figures 3–4; v1 has no comparable implementation or code-access information. Figure 5’s detailed setups are delegated to cited papers.

R1.justification: Positioning shifts from making minimal changes to existing uncertainty discussions toward unifying them through decision theory. v2 substantially adds decision-theory, model-selection and estimation literature, including Dawid, DeGroot, Neiswanger and Huang, while removing much of v1’s engineering-history discussion and associated references.

P1.justification: The introduction, key-concept exposition, alternative perspective and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Sections 3 and 5 become detailed numbered subsections, the former related-work section is integrated into Background, and examples, proofs and implementation details are organized into three appendices.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the earlier decomposition schematic with a broader decision-theory diagram, revises and renumbers v1’s ambiguity diagram as Figure 2, and adds experimental Figures 3–5. Main text and references change from single-column to two-column layout, while appendices use full-width presentation.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly acknowledged abstracting away dependence on the actual data and learning algorithm. v2 addresses that important limitation through its policy- and update-dependent framework, clarifies estimator assumptions, and adds original demonstrations with implementation details. These changes substantially strengthen precision and evidential support, despite limited local documentation of Figure 5’s experimental settings.
